newsitem.title: INDIA: PRESS DIGEST - INDIAN NEWSPAPERS - AUGUST 8.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - INDIAN NEWSPAPERS - AUGUST 8.

text.p: Following is a summary of major Indian business and political stories in leading newspapers prepared for Reuters by Business News and Information Services Pvt Ltd, New Delhi Tel:3324842, 3351006, 3761233 Fax:+91-11-3351006 Internet: biznis@giasbm01.vsnl.net.in
Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
TOP STORIES
Indian Express
OPPOSITION PARTY BLOCKS ANOTHER BILL

The opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) forced the defeat of a government-backed bill to amend the Presidential and Vice-presidential Elections Act of 1952 in the upper house of parliament. Prime Minister Gujral in the evening pleaded with the BJP to pass the bill but BJP members Satish Aggarwal and Vijay Kumar Malhotra insisted that the statutory resolution they moved earlier in the day disapproving the ordinance should be put to vote. The government did not press for a division of heads in the voice vote since the Congress party benches were empty with its members attending a party session in Calcutta. Minister of State of Home Maqbool Dar was also forced to withdraw a bill on private security guards and agencies.
The Hindustan Times
KESRI UNDER PRESSURE TO HOLD WORKING COMMITTEE POLLS

Top Congress party leaders barring those who are close to party President Sitaram Kesri pressed for a poll to elect a new Congress Working Committee. Kesri's supporters were unable to mobilise enough support for authorising him to nominate members to the Working Committee. Prominent among those who were favouring an open contest were party vice president Jitendra Prasada, Sharad Pawar and Arjun Singh, and those who were opposed to this were led by Pranab Mukherjee. Kesari said after a party steering committee meeting he would not stand in the way of elections to the Congress Working committee.
The Economic Times
BOURSE INDICATOR FALLS BY 76 POINTS

The Bombay stock market shed 75.95 points as pivotals slid on rumours that Finance Minister P. Chidambaram was considering resigning. Sensing the change in sentiment, bull operators started liquidating their positions. Foreign institutional investors turned cautious before enlarging large-scale commitments. The sensitive index tumbled to close at 4,447.06 points.
GUJRAL TO SEEK OPPOSITION HELP TO SAVE INSURANCE BILL

Sources said there were positive signs that the Insurance Regulatory Authority bill could be salvaged and reintroduced with a few amendments in the present session of parliament itself. The bill may be reintroduced in parliament before August 14. The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which forced the government to withdraw the bill, may agree to support it. BJP leader Jaswant Singh is in touch with Finance Minister P. Chidambaram. BJP leader A.B. Vajpayee is believed to have admitted that since the General Insurance Corporation operated in 35 countries, it was improper to introduce an amendment saying no foreign insurance company could be allowed to operate in the Indian market.
Financial Express
MORGAN STANLEY PICKS UP PART OF ASIAN PAINTS' EQUITY

U.S. investment bank Morgan Stanley picked up a part of Asian Paints' stake sold by managing director Atul Choksey. Morgan Stanley is believed to have picked up three percent of Choksey's holdings while five percent was picked up by Capital International. Morgan Stanley refused to comment on the deal. Morgan Stanley's association with the deal, which set Asian Paints' stock afire on the market last week, is significant given the bank's penchant for parking operations. It could mean that sooner or later Morgan would be looking for a buyer for the stake.
VAZIR SULTAN TOBACCO SEEKS NOD TO HIKE BAT'S STAKE

The Vazir Sultan Tobacco Industries has sought the permission of the Foreign Investment Promotion Board to hike the foreign equity stake held by two subsidiaries of the British American Tobacco company to 50 percent. The subsidiaries now hold a 31.73 percent stake. The Andhra Pradesh state government, which holds 4.7 percent stake, has supported the proposal. The company's application states that the equity increase will be effected through purchase of the unsubscribed portion of the proposed 750 million rupee rights issue of the Vazir Sultan Tobacco Industries.
Business Standard
PLAN TO ALLOW 100 PCT MULTINATIONAL TRADING FIRMS

The government is formulating a policy that will allow overseas companies to set up wholly owned subsidiaries to undertake trading activities in India. It will allow multinational companies to set up wholly owned subsidiaries to trade in specific products like speciality chemicals but ban some other product categories which could directly compete with those made by domestic players. The policy will try to place certain minimum conditions that the subsidiary will have to meet regarding location of outlets, pricing, sourcing (including import of products) and their sale.
CAR FIRMS' EXPORT ONUS TO BE EASED

The Commerce Ministry finalised a new policy for signing memoranda of understanding with automobile companies and issuing licences to import completely knocked down and semi-knocked down auto kits. The new policy will not include any duty concessions on kit imports, said Commerce Minister B.B. Ramaiah. It will include an easier export obligation period and allow exports of auto components and ancillaries instead of just cars. The minister said the guidelines would not need cabinet approval since no new duty concessions would be included.
The Observer
INSURANCE INDUSTRY WANTS CURBS ON OVERSEAS COMPANIES

Indian insurance industry leaders said they wanted an end to a state monopoly in the sector but no free access to overseas firms. They said overseas companies must be restricted to minority shareholdings in private joint ventures. Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) President N. Kumar said the insurance sector needed urgent liberalisation but Indian firms should have a majority stake in insurance joint ventures. He said the CII backed the recommendations of a committee that foreign investors should be allowed in the business but sought extra safeguards for the Indian firms. The government on Wednesday had to withdraw an insurance regulatory bill following pressure from the opposition in parliament.
COURT SAYS ANTI-DUMPING DUTY ON NEWSPRINT IS IN ORDER

The Delhi High court Thursday dismissed petitions by four newspapers that challenged a recommendation to impose anti-dumping duty on imported newsprint. The court said no case was made out at this stage for the interference of the court in the matter. The petition was dismissed without issuing notice to the respondents. The government counsel told the court that it was only a recommendation to the government and it might or might not impose the duty. Anti-dumping duty on imported newsprint was recommended by a designated authority in the Commerce Ministry.
Business Line
INSURANCE REGULATORY BILL WILL BE REINTRODUCED

The government said the Insurance Regulatory Authority bill would be reintroduced in parliament after another round of consultations with the political parties who forced its withdrawal on Wednesday. V.K. Dhall, additional secretary (insurance) in the Finance Ministry, said the failure of the bill in parliament should be seen in the right perspective by the insurance community.
FOREIGN INSURERS UNFAZED

Overseas insurers expressed their strong commitment to the Indian market and said they would not review their plans to enter the insurance sector because the Insurance Regulatory Authority bill had been withdrawn. A section of the global insurance majors felt such setbacks were inevitable in a democratic system. Mark Boleat, director general of the Association of British Insurers, said the withdrawal of the bill was not an indication of the derailment of the reform process. William A. Barr, managing director of the Guardian Insurance Services, said he believed liberalisation of the economy in general and that of the insurance sector in particular still remained a policy of the government.
